facts: I estimate that I first started using AI for programming one to two years before the original interview, but am unsure because I did not adopt it immediately when my company introduced it.

My personal AI programming use began roughly a year before the original interview, possibly slightly less or more. My company had provided AI for longer than a year, so I selected the one-to-two-year range with uncertainty.
At work we have access to browser-based ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot.
I confirmed that AI is integrated directly into my IDE.
AI is always integrated into my Visual Studio environment as a plugin.
I mainly use AI for unit tests because I dislike writing them, and for documentation. I sometimes use AI for debugging depending on the problem.
I rarely use AI to write actual code, but recently used it several times to generate code quickly for a regulatory project with a very strict deadline.
I used AI code generation on that regulatory project because of the strict deadline; normally I dislike AI-generated code because I often find its quality poor.
I rate AI use for writing or generating code as rare.
I sometimes use AI for debugging and understanding unfamiliar code, and rarely for refactoring; exceptional projects can require more AI code generation.
I use AI often, even very often, for writing tests.
I use AI very often for documentation.
I sometimes use AI for explaining concepts and learning.
In a normal programming task I first receive and read the requirements, open Visual Studio and inspect the code relevant to the functionality.
My normal workflow differs depending on whether I know the code. For unfamiliar code I usually debug it myself line by line to see what happens.
For unfamiliar business-oriented flows I may use internal tools with real-life data, such as the developer portal or Swagger requests for APIs, to observe the actual flow.
After analyzing the code and relevant business flow, I think through the problem and begin coding.

For complicated tasks I may create a small project or design notes for myself; for simple tasks I start coding directly. After writing code I usually run it locally or use external tools such as Swagger. Sometimes I deploy my branch through pipelines and test it through internal API access tools, then check the PR quality gates.

For pull-request quality checks we use SonarQube for code quality and Veracode for security. We rarely have Veracode problems, but I find some SonarQube rules objectionable. At the end I check existing unit tests and modify them myself if changing existing functionality.
For completely new functionality I usually ask AI to write unit tests and then verify them. If SonarQube complains about missing documentation in particular places, I may ask AI to add it.

How tasks arrive depends on the requester. Ideally requirements are well described in our internal wiki, but often I still clarify them in meetings or direct conversations, keep my own notes and sometimes add them to the wiki.
Sometimes someone requests a small task directly, and I create a Team Foundation Server item myself. Every task needs a TFS item, but the requirements are often not recorded in that item.
General activity frequency varies by time of year; averaging across periods, I rate reviewing code as often.
I consider bug fixing and debugging to be two distinct activities rather than one category.

For me debugging includes learning about a flow, searching and investigating possible bugs without necessarily writing code. Bug fixing means I already know what is wrong and physically fix it, usually by writing code.
I regard debugging primarily as investigation, which is why I distinguish it from bug fixing.

I debug often because my team has support duty and owns many APIs; we sometimes investigate problems even if another team is responsible for the fix. Actual bug fixing within the year before the original interview was almost never.
Our team has a dedicated QA member, so developers generally do a smoke test before handing work over to QA.
We developers smoke-test every task, but it takes a very small share of time, so I was unsure how to rate it.
I revised the running-tests frequency to sometimes because we have a dedicated tester, although I personally always do it and some teammates do not.
I work with requirements very often, essentially always.
Documentation is part of the task process, but I do not always add it and may skip it if nobody asks.
I rate documentation as sometimes in my normal work.
I rate continuous learning often, though it depends on the task: some tasks require much new learning and others involve things I already know.
Working with requirements and unit testing take most of my time regardless of AI use. Requirements are time-consuming because they require clarification with different people.
I dislike unit testing, which I mentioned while explaining why it takes much of my time.
I find the relevant work, especially the unit testing discussed here, definitely faster with AI.
A recent requirements task began with reading a wiki page describing requirements and inspecting a code base belonging to another service, which I had to learn.

For the recent requirements task I had to learn additional business knowledge, attend repeated clarification meetings, reanalyze requirements and code, discuss data-quality problems privately with the requirements owner and in another meeting, and investigate whether QA's reported issues originated in the unfamiliar service code.

Near the end of the recent requirements task, business stakeholders changed requirements after I had stopped coding, so I had to rewrite the code. We then discovered existing service bugs that were not compliant with regulatory requirements.

In my company it is common to return to requirements during implementation because they change, requiring code rewrites. I would prefer requirements to be settled up front, but that is not our reality.
Repeated clarification and changes during implementation are why working with requirements is so time-consuming for me.
For the recent regulatory requirements task I used AI because it concerned regulations transcribed as MFID and financial matters I knew nothing about, with a tight deadline.
On the regulatory cost-calculation task I used AI to learn about the regulations transcribed as MFID and quickly check economic and mathematical calculations.
I used AI to explain the cost calculations more quickly while examining the actual code.
For the regulatory calculation task I also used ordinary programming tools, including my IDE and SQL Management Studio to inspect data.
Talking with people took the longest in my recent regulatory requirements task.
I estimate that roughly half my work involves code I did not write or unfamiliar parts of the code base.

My team owns numerous services, some with old and new versions, and I did not write most of them. We are several developers with nominal responsibility for individual services, but larger services involve multiple contributors; about half the time I work on features, fixes or investigations in code written by others.
Even within our team's own services I may know other parts but not the specific part needing a change. During bug investigations we are sometimes assigned problems outside our team's services.
My team tends to investigate deeply, sometimes examining other teams' code; many of my colleagues use Copilot to explore unfamiliar code.
My colleagues use AI to understand unfamiliar code during investigations such as debugging. I began contrasting this with writing a feature.

In my experience many senior programmers my age or older prefer investigating with their own reasoning, whereas younger colleagues tend to use AI more often. This is my observation, not a universal claim.
When modifying someone else's code, we rely on unit tests, integration tests called L2 tests, and smoke tests to avoid breaking functionality.
After developers change code, they perform development tests and our QA team tests the full functionality before merging and releasing.

Another AI-assisted example was within the same regulatory feature: we discovered rounding problems in mathematical calculations across the application. My own task concerned only a small feature, and I lacked time to inspect the whole application.

The regulatory rounding issue affected our numbers but originated deeper in the endpoint than my small feature. I used AI to investigate the mathematical calculations rather than immediately learning the entire endpoint.
The rounding problem involved several complicated code locations. To investigate it I gave AI a set of actual live data from the application, as I reported in the interview.

I suspected a rounding problem in the regulatory cost-calculation endpoint and gave AI the observed data while asking about applicable industry regulations and standards for calculating and rounding costs. I quickly found that the original code was not aligned with the regulation I referred to as MFID. I had not used that regulation before but had already suspected the cause.
AI did not fundamentally change my analysis process for the rounding issue. Without it I would ask the same regulatory questions but seek answers from people or browser searches.
Without AI I would use conventional resources such as Stack Overflow; I suppose AI also draws on publicly available resources. The AI-assisted route was much faster.
For the regulatory rounding task, doing the same analytical steps manually would have taken much longer.

I always validate AI output because I have seen it generate very poor code. My company uses externally based models including GPT integrated into our IDE with external connections restricted, as well as internally trained models; I have observed different answers from different models.
I find AI can give good answers for simple changes such as rewriting a one- or two-line condition, but it often handles complex applications poorly when overall composition and business logic matter.
I do not like using AI very frequently for programming.

I have always enjoyed programming because solving puzzles, locating problems and rebuilding things are pleasant mental activities. I believe this trains my brain, and worry that relying on AI constantly would erode that ability.

I avoid constant AI reliance because I value trained analytical thinking. I have observed younger colleagues who rely heavily on AI sometimes struggle to comprehend problems that feel natural to me; this is my personal assessment.

I nevertheless appreciate AI for situations like the recent unfamiliar regulatory project, where the legal deadline was short and missing it could incur a fine. AI was helpful, but its output still needed verification.
For the recent regulatory task I found AI very useful for understanding mathematical and regulatory matters.

entries.topic: 大语言模型与提示注入
entries.text: 大语言模型与提示注入应作概念区分：大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型；提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
强化学习与测试集应作概念区分：强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略；测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
精确率与上下文窗口应作概念区分：精确率是预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例；上下文窗口是模型单次推理能够处理的输入输出词元范围。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
代码审查与模型幻觉应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
代码审查与单元测试应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
上下文窗口（context window）：模型单次推理能够处理的输入输出词元范围。
大语言模型（large language model）：从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型。
持续集成（continuous integration）：每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。

entries.topic: 持续集成与无监督学习
entries.text: 持续集成与无监督学习应作概念区分：持续集成是每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程；无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

训练集（training set）：用于拟合模型参数的数据样本。

监督学习与验证集应作概念区分：监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射；验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
提示注入与单元测试应作概念区分：提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令；单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
数据泄漏与精确率应作概念区分：数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息；精确率是预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
模型幻觉与监督学习应作概念区分：模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象；监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
欠拟合与召回率应作概念区分：欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分；召回率是实际为正的样本中被正确识别的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
